head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Iterative inorder traversal: go left as far as possible, then process, then go right
The previously visited node, so adjacent values can be compared
In a BST (Binary Search Tree) the inorder sequence must be increasing, so a drop marks a misplaced pair
first = prev (only the first time); second = node (every time)
The first violation's larger value, and the last violation's smaller value
Swapping the two values repairs the tree without relinking

p: Tree `[1,3,null,null,2]` (1's left child 3, whose right child is 2). Inorder visits 3, 2, 1:
bullets: first = 3, second = 1: swapping their values gives a valid BST.

p: If the two swapped nodes are adjacent in inorder there is ONE inversion, and first/second are that pair. If they are far apart there are TWO inversions: the first inversion's larger value is the misplaced big one, and the second inversion's smaller value is the misplaced small one. Setting `second` on every inversion makes it end at the later one.

bullets: Space: O(h) for the stack. Morris traversal (temporary threading) reduces it to O(1).

99.takeaway: Inorder of a BST must be increasing; the first drop's larger node and the last drop's smaller node are the swapped pair.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Orders people by how much cheaper city A is than city B (most negative first)
Exactly half go to each city
The n people who prefer A most go to A; the rest go to B

p: Suppose everyone first flies to city B; the cost is the sum of all B costs. Sending a person to A changes the total by `costA − costB`. We must send exactly n people to A, so we choose the n with the smallest (most negative) differences. That is an exchange argument: any other choice has a larger total change.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort.
Space: O(n) for the sorted copy.

1029.takeaway: Greedy by cost difference: send the n people with the smallest A − B to city A.

What it does

rows: Combines the three lists into tuples and sorts by time (timestamp is first), restoring each user's visit order
Per-user list of sites in time order
From `itertools`: every 3-element subsequence in original order (not contiguous)
Each user counts a pattern once, however many times they visited it
min(p for p, c in cnt.items() if c == best)
Among the most frequent patterns, the lexicographically smallest tuple

p: Per-user visit sequences after sorting by time:
bullets: Highest user count is 2; the smallest of those patterns is `['home', 'about', 'career']`.

p: The score of a pattern is the number of different users who visited it. If a user visited `home → about → career` three times, they still count once. The set removes the repeats before counting.

bullets: Time: O(N log N + Σ C(m, 3)) for N visits, where m is a user's visit count; the combinations term dominates for users with many visits.
Space: O of the number of distinct patterns.

1152.takeaway: Group visits by user in time order, count each 3-site subsequence once per user, return the most common (lexicographically smallest on ties).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Number of ways to reach sum s with the dice rolled so far
Zero dice make sum 0 in one way
The last die shows 1..k but cannot exceed the target sum so far
Ways to reach s: ways to reach s − f with one fewer die, over every face f
Keeps numbers small as the problem asks (10⁹+7)

p: `n = 2`, `k = 6`, `target = 7`; index = sum:

blocks.h: Why a fresh `new` array each round?
p: Each die must be counted exactly once. Updating `dp` in place would let the same die contribute more than once to a sum in a round. Building `new` from the previous round's `dp` keeps one die per round.

1155.takeaway: Dice-sum DP: new[s] = Σ over faces f of old[s − f], one array per die.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Turns the list into a min-heap in O(n); the smallest stick is always at index 0
Takes the smallest item in O(log n)
Joining two sticks costs their combined length

blocks.h: Why always merge the two smallest?
p: Every merge cost is paid again each time the merged stick is merged later, so long sticks should be merged as few times as possible. This is the same greedy as Huffman coding: repeatedly combining the two smallest minimizes the total weighted cost.

bullets: Space: O(1) extra (the heap reuses the input list).

1167.takeaway: Huffman-style greedy with a min-heap: always merge the two shortest sticks.

Acquires the lock for the block, releases it on exit (even after an exception)
A full queue: releases the lock and sleeps until notified, then re-checks the condition

p: Capacity 2. A real run of this code (the third enqueue ran in a separate thread):

head: step

rows: blocks while the queue is full

p: When a waiting thread wakes up, another thread may have already filled (or emptied) the queue again, or the wake-up may be spurious. With `while`, the condition is re-checked after every wake-up and the thread goes back to sleep if it still cannot proceed. `if` would let it continue with a stale assumption.

bullets: Time: O(1) per operation when it does not block.

1188.takeaway: Condition variable with while-wait loops: producers wait while full, consumers wait while empty, both notify after changing the queue.

BFS (Breadth-First Search) one layer per move, so `steps` is the move count
Shortest path in an unweighted graph
A small margin around the target: the path may need to step slightly outside the quadrant

p: Target (5, 5). Number of squares in each BFS layer:

blocks.h: Why the margin of 2 and not a tight box?
p: The shortest route to a corner can need a step to a square with a negative coordinate, for example to reach (1, 1). A margin of 2 beyond the target on each side (and −2 below zero) keeps all useful squares while bounding the search.

bullets: Time: O(x · y) squares in the bounded area.

1197.takeaway: BFS from the origin over knight moves, restricted to a small box around the target by symmetry.

Every pair with that gap, already in ascending order

p: If a < b < c, then c − a is larger than both c − b and b − a. So a pair with elements between them can never have the smallest difference, and checking neighbours after sorting is enough.

1200.takeaway: Sort, then the smallest gap must be between neighbours; collect every neighbour pair with that gap.

p: `"deeedbbcccbdaa"`, k = 3:

blocks.h: Why store counts in the stack?
p: Without the counts, every removal would need to rescan the string to see whether a run of k exists. The stack keeps the count of the current run, so the check is O(1) and a removal immediately exposes the previous run with its own count.

A balanced prefix has just ended; cut here
Greedy: cut at the earliest chance

p: `"RLRRLLRLRL"`:

blocks.h: Why cut at the first zero?

Only follow links on the same host
Provided API that returns the links found on a page

p: A small site: the start page links to a page on its own host and to another host:
Pages link to each other in cycles. Without `seen` the crawler would revisit the same pages forever. Marking a URL when it is queued (not when it is processed) also prevents duplicates in the queue.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Map from a letter-set bitmask to the longest concatenation length using exactly that set; the empty set has length 0
Bitmask representation of a set of letters
Detects a repeated letter inside the word itself
The word's letters are disjoint from the existing set, so it can be appended
Iterates a snapshot so new entries are not processed in the same round

bullets: `un` + `iq` = 4 letters is the best; `un` and `ue` share `u`, so they cannot be combined.

blocks.h: Why a dict of masks and not recursion over subsets?
p: The number of distinct letter sets is bounded by 2^26, but in practice only a few are reachable. The dict visits just those, and each word is processed once per existing set, which is much smaller than trying all subsets of words.

bullets: Time: O(n · reachable masks), at most O(n · 2^26) but small in practice.

1239.takeaway: Bitmask DP in a dict: extend every reachable letter set by each word whose letters are unique and disjoint.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A pool of 4 worker threads that run tasks concurrently; `with` shuts it down cleanly
Fetches every page of the current level in parallel, returning results in the input order
Level-by-level BFS (Breadth-First Search): all pages of one level are fetched together
Updated only in the main thread, after results are back, so no lock is needed

p: A small site (the parallel fetches happen inside each level):

head: frontier (fetched in parallel)
new pages for the next level

bullets: Pages kept: http://news.yahoo.com/about, http://news.yahoo.com/news, http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/ (the google.com link is on a different host).

blocks.h: Why is it safe without locks?
p: Only `getUrls` runs in the worker threads and it returns data. All reads and writes of `seen` and `nxt` happen in the main thread while consuming the results of `pool.map`. Since no two threads touch the same mutable structure, there is no race.

bullets: Time: about (number of levels) × (slowest fetch in each level) instead of the sum of all fetches.

1242.takeaway: Level-synchronous BFS: fetch each level in parallel with a thread pool, update the visited set only in the main thread.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges
Adjacency list for an undirected tree
Breadth-first distances from s; returns the farthest node and its distance
Single-source shortest paths in an unweighted tree
A node at the maximum distance
The first from any node finds one end of a longest path, the second from that end measures the diameter

blocks.h: Why does the double sweep work?
p: In a tree, the node farthest from ANY starting node is an endpoint of some longest path. Starting again from that endpoint, the farthest node is the other endpoint, and its distance is the diameter. This holds only for trees (it fails with weighted negative edges or in general graphs).

bullets: Time: O(n) with two BFS runs.

1245.takeaway: Tree diameter by two BFS runs: farthest node from anywhere, then farthest from that node.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Running number of odd numbers: turns the array into 0/1 and uses prefix sums
How many prefixes had each odd-count; the empty prefix has 0 odd numbers
Earlier prefixes with exactly k fewer odd numbers: each gives a subarray with exactly k odd numbers
Records the current prefix after counting

blocks.h: Why is this the same as the 'subarray sum equals k' problem?
p: Replace each number by `x % 2`. A subarray has exactly k odd numbers iff its 0/1 sum is k. Prefix sums with a counter give the number of subarrays with a given sum in one pass.

1248.takeaway: Map to 0/1 (odd), then count subarrays with sum k using prefix sums and a counter.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Iterative DFS (Depth-First Search) with an explicit stack that turns a connected group of 0s (land) into 1s (water)
Only land inside the grid is filled; stack entries outside are discarded when popped
Land touching the border cannot be a closed island; flooding it first removes it
Eliminate the cases that don't count
Each remaining 0 starts a closed island: count it and flood it so it is counted once

p: Here 0 is land and 1 is water. Cells filled from the border: [(0, 7, '3 cells'), (4, 7, '1 cells')].

An island is closed only if water (1) surrounds it completely, so a land group touching the edge is not closed. Flooding all border land beforehand lets the second pass count every remaining group without checking its edges.

1254.takeaway: Flood the border land first, then count the remaining land components.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Consecutive pairs of points in visiting order
Chebyshev distance: with diagonal moves allowed, the time is the larger of the two

p: Each second you can change x by 1, y by 1, or both. Diagonal steps cover both directions at once, so the time to cover (dx, dy) is the larger of the two; the sum would be right only if diagonal moves were not allowed (Manhattan distance).

1266.takeaway: With diagonal moves, the travel time between points is max(|dx|, |dy|); sum over consecutive legs.
